strengths: Proposes a novel problem-oriented perspective for code optimization, shifting from same-user iterative pairs to pairs formed from different programmers' solutions to the same problem, which encourages global algorithmic innovation rather than local edits.

Constructs and releases PIE-Problem, a new training dataset with 14,051 pairs over 336 problems, and provides analysis showing that a much higher proportion of pairs involve global algorithmic optimizations compared to the original PIE-User dataset.
Conducts extensive experiments across multiple Code LLMs (CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B and DeepSeek-Coder 7B/33B), with baselines including instruct prompting, CoT, self-correct, and curriculum learning.

Shows substantial empirical gains when fine-tuning on PIE-Problem: e.g., DeepSeek-Coder 33B improves %OPT from 51.76% to 71.03% and speedup from 2.649x to 4.812x under BEST@8 relative to PIE-User fine-tuning.
Identifies the correctness bottleneck of problem-oriented fine-tuning and applies model merging (Linear/Slerp) to improve the trade-off, with a merge-weight analysis for different lambda values.
Uses gem5 simulator for deterministic execution-time measurement and unit tests for correctness, supporting reliable and reproducible evaluation.
Provides error analysis and optimization-type categorization, offering useful insights into failure modes and dataset characteristics.
weaknesses: Evaluation mismatch: the test set remains the original user-oriented PIE test pairs. No problem-oriented test set is constructed to directly evaluate the claimed perspective, so the model is not tested on optimizing code from a different programmer, which is the core of the proposed setting.

Confounded comparison between PIE-User and PIE-Problem fine-tuning: PIE-User uses performance-conditioned generation while PIE-Problem uses a simple instruction. It is unclear how much of the improvement is due to the data perspective versus the prompt difference; a controlled same-prompt comparison is missing.

Dataset construction is unclear and notationally inconsistent. The trajectory Y_x^p and pair generation are ambiguous (e.g., sorting by execution time versus first submissions), and the >90% improvement threshold is arbitrary and not ablated, potentially biasing training toward extreme speedups.

The final headline improvement (51.76% -> 76.65% %OPT, 2.65x -> 5.09x speedup) relies on merging the PIE-Problem model with the PIE-User model, so the gain is not solely from the problem-oriented perspective. The abstract may overstate the contribution of the new perspective.

Model merging details are insufficient for reproducibility (e.g., whether LoRA adapters or full weights are merged, Slerp hyperparameters), and the merging method itself is off-the-shelf rather than a novel technical contribution.
No statistical significance testing or variance estimates (e.g., multiple seeds, confidence intervals) despite a relatively small test set of 80 problems / 1,422 pairs and many model comparisons.
Lacks a simple combined-data baseline, such as multi-task training on PIE-User + PIE-Problem, which would help isolate the benefit of the problem-oriented perspective.
Writing quality issues: typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'Tale 2', 't is important', 'Deepseek-Coder 33b'), undefined notation, and occasional unclear phrasing reduce clarity for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses the important and under-explored problem of LLM-based code optimization for execution time.
It proposes a problem-oriented reorganization of the PIE dataset, which is a reasonable idea for exposing models to diverse algorithmic solutions.
The empirical study is broad, covering multiple Code LLMs and parameter scales, and uses the deterministic gem5 simulator for timing, which improves reproducibility.
The paper provides error analysis and merge-weight analysis, and promises to release dataset/code/scripts.
weaknesses: The central comparison is confounded: PIE-Problem pairs require >90% relative improvement while PIE-User pairs require >10%. The performance gains may stem from the stricter threshold (more aggressive optimization targets) rather than the problem-oriented perspective itself. No controlled experiment matches thresholds or constructs problem-oriented pairs with a 10% threshold.

The evaluation still uses the original user-oriented validation/test sets (same-user iterative pairs), so the paper never actually evaluates inference on problem-oriented pairs. The claimed problem-oriented perspective is only used for training, not tested for cross-user optimization.

Model merging is an existing technique, and the paper does not compare against the natural baseline of training on the union of PIE-User and PIE-Problem data (or multi-task training). It also does not compare against other merging methods beyond Linear and SLERP.
The merge weight λ appears to be analyzed and possibly selected on the test set (Figure 5), with no clear validation-based selection protocol. This risks overfitting the test set.

The novelty is limited: the main contributions are a data reorganization of an existing dataset and applying known model-merging methods. There is no new optimization algorithm, model architecture, or training objective.

There is a lack of ablation on dataset size and pair quality: PIE-Problem has far fewer problems and pairs than PIE-User, so the attribution to 'high-quality global pairs' versus simply different data distribution is not isolated.

The final merged model still has much lower correctness than the PIE-User baseline (e.g., 78.76% vs 91.14% for DeepSeek-Coder 33B), and the paper does not adequately analyze the correctness-performance trade-off or the practical acceptability of 25% compilation failures.

The paper's claims are stronger than the evidence: it asserts a 'problem-oriented perspective' but only demonstrates improved metrics on user-oriented test pairs. The title and abstract imply a broader shift than what is empirically validated.

strengths: Introduces a novel problem-oriented perspective for constructing code optimization pairs by reusing submissions from different programmers for the same problem, and releases PIE-Problem as a new dataset.
Provides a broad empirical study across CodeLlama and DeepSeek-Coder at multiple scales, with prompt, CoT, LoRA fine-tuning, BEST@1 and BEST@8, showing consistent and substantial gains over PIE-User.
Evaluation setup is relatively careful: deterministic gem5 timing, unit-test correctness, same validation/test sets, and multiple metrics plus error and merge-weight analyses.

Model merging (Merge-Linear / Merge-Slerp) is shown to mitigate the correctness bottleneck of PIE-Problem training and improves final %OPT and speedup; compared against self-correction and curriculum learning.
The dataset construction and optimization-type analysis (GPT-4 and human) provide useful evidence that PIE-Problem contains more global algorithmic optimizations than PIE-User.
Reproducibility is supported by public dataset/code/evaluation scripts, detailed training hyperparameters, prompts, and error analysis.
weaknesses: The central comparison confounds the problem-oriented perspective with the 90% relative-improvement threshold: PIE-Problem pairs are much more aggressive than PIE-User pairs, and no controlled experiment filters PIE-User pairs to a comparable threshold or matches speedup distributions, so the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to cross-programmer diversity.
The 90% threshold is arbitrary and its sensitivity is not studied; it may discard useful moderate global optimizations and biases the dataset toward a particular notion of global optimization.

Dataset construction is largely a re-pairing and re-ranking of existing PIE/CodeNet submissions, which limits the novelty of the dataset contribution, and some constructed pairs still come from the same user.
Model merging is used somewhat heuristically; the paper does not deeply analyze why merging improves correctness or compare against alternative ensembles/reranking/self-consistency strategies.

Correctness remains a serious practical limitation: final Best@8 correct rate is only about 78.8%, and the merged model is less correct than the PIE-User fine-tuned model; for real code optimization, incorrect but fast outputs are not deployable.
The evaluation is limited to C++ competitive-programming time optimization; generalizability to other languages, software domains, memory optimization, and larger systems is not demonstrated.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., significantly enhances optimization capabilities and overcomes bottlenecks, while the main confound and remaining correctness gap are not fully resolved.

strengths: Introduces a problem-oriented perspective for constructing code optimization pairs, addressing the limitation of user-oriented iterative pairs and showing substantial empirical gains across multiple LLMs (e.g., %OPT 31.24%→58.89%, SPEEDUP 2.95×→5.22×).

Provides multi-dimensional analyses (CFG graph edit distance, semantic embeddings, human/GPT-4 sampling) to support the claim that problem-oriented pairs contain more global algorithmic changes and greater semantic diversity.

Proposes anchor verification, a simple and effective refinement mechanism that uses the functionally correct slow code as a test-case oracle; it improves correctness and downstream optimization across QWEN2.5-CODER, GPT-4o, and DEEPSEEK-V3.
Extensive experiments span multiple model families/scales, BEST@1/BEST@8, PCO percentage data-efficiency analysis, and comparisons with self-debugging and direct test generation.
Problem-level train/validation/test splitting reduces leakage risk, and the appendix includes detailed training configurations, prompts, and implementation settings.
Demonstrates practical data efficiency: with only 30% of PCO pairs, fine-tuned LLMs can surpass full PIE performance on %OPT and SPEEDUP.
weaknesses: PCO construction retains the same number of pairs per problem as PIE by selecting top-speedup pairs, rather than using all or randomly sampled problem-oriented pairs. This selection confound may inflate the reported PCO gains and does not cleanly isolate the effect of the problem-oriented perspective.

The claimed scale/quantity advantage is inconsistent with the actual construction: the formulas count all pairwise combinations, while the method uses sequential/adjacent pairs and then subsamples to 78K pairs, so the extra quantity bonus is not substantiated.
The test set is small (41 problems, 978 pairs), and the paper reports no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests; variance could affect conclusions.

Anchor verification uses only three generated test inputs in Stage 1 and a maximum of one refinement iteration; there is no ablation on the number/coverage of generated tests, number of iterations, or filtering failures, limiting understanding of its robustness.
The baseline comparisons for anchor verification are limited to self-debugging and direct test generation; other verification/test-generation strategies or no-refinement evaluations are not explored.

Novelty is moderate: reordering submissions by runtime across users and using slow code as a test oracle are straightforward engineering/data-centric ideas rather than fundamentally new technical contributions.

The manuscript has presentation issues, including reference formatting errors, typos (e.g., “SeepSeek-AI”, “Kistler and Franchini”), an inconsistent pair-counting formula, and some unclear examples of how problem-oriented pairs are formed.
Strong claims such as “elevates both the optimization ratio and speedup to new levels” are not fully supported given the selection confound, small test set, and limited ablations.

strengths: Addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: using LLMs for execution-time code optimization beyond what optimizing compilers provide.

The problem-oriented dataset perspective is simple and intuitive: pooling submissions from multiple programmers for the same problem can expose more diverse and globally different optimization strategies.
The empirical results are fairly consistent across several base models, showing that fine-tuning on PCO improves %OPT, speedup, and correctness relative to PIE fine-tuning.

The anchor verification mechanism is a reasonable practical idea: using the original slow but correct program as a test oracle is more reliable than asking an LLM to synthesize both inputs and expected outputs.

The paper includes several analyses (GED, t-SNE, human/GPT sampling, percentage-of-data study, refinement ablations) that attempt to characterize the differences between user-oriented and problem-oriented pairs.
weaknesses: The central comparison between PIE and PCO is confounded. PCO is constructed by selecting the top-speedup pairs per problem, while PIE appears to use the original sequential user pairs. This means PCO may simply contain much stronger optimization pairs by construction, not because of the problem-oriented perspective itself. A controlled comparison with matched speedup distributions, random problem-oriented pairs, or top-speedup user-oriented pairs is needed.

The novelty is limited. Re-sorting submissions from multiple users by runtime and pairing them is a straightforward dataset re-organization, and the anchor verification mechanism is essentially differential testing against a reference implementation. Neither is a fundamental methodological advance for a top-tier AI conference.

The evaluation is narrow: only C++ competitive-programming problems from CodeNet, with a small test set (41 problems/978 pairs). There is no evaluation on real-world repositories, other languages, or other performance dimensions such as memory usage.

The 'anchor verification' framing overclaims. It does not verify functional equivalence; it only checks a handful of LLM-generated inputs (e.g., three test cases) with one refinement iteration. This can easily overfit to generated tests and still fail on unseen inputs.

Experimental details for Table 2 are unclear and potentially confounded. It is not clear whether GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 are generating optimized code or only refining Qwen outputs, and the same baseline is used across all three backbones. This makes the refinement comparison hard to interpret.

Important ablations are missing. The paper does not isolate the effect of cross-user pairs from the effect of top-speedup selection, nor does it compare against simpler baselines such as using public/CodeNet test cases, random tests, or compiler/perf tools. The percentage analysis still relies on the top-selected PCO pairs.

Claims are stronger than the evidence: 'first to introduce a problem-oriented perspective,' 'anchor verification,' and 'elevates to new levels' are not supported by the controlled experiments. The mechanism does not guarantee correctness, and the correctness metric is based on the available test cases only.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Training details omit important hyperparameters such as batch size, sequence length, LoRA configuration specifics beyond lora_rank/lora_target, and the publicly available code link is not provided in the manuscript. There are also citation/reference errors and formatting issues, including a stray problem statement and broken-looking figure/reference artifacts.

Potential contamination and benchmark concerns are unaddressed. The base LLMs may have seen CodeNet or similar competitive-programming problems during pretraining, and no contamination analysis is provided for either PIE or PCO.

strengths: The problem-oriented perspective is simple but effective: aggregating valid submissions from multiple programmers for the same problem broadens the optimization trajectory and appears to encourage more global algorithmic changes than user-oriented pairs.

The paper provides useful multi-dimensional analysis (CFG edit distance, semantic embeddings, human/LLM sampling) comparing problem-oriented and user-oriented pairs, supporting the claim that PCO pairs involve more substantial structural changes.

Empirical results are strong and consistent across multiple Code LLMs: fine-tuning on PCO substantially improves %OPT, speedup, and correctness compared with PIE, and using only 30% of PCO pairs still surpasses full PIE in some metrics, demonstrating data efficiency.

The anchor verification framework is a reasonable and practical solution to the optimization tax: using the original slow code as a correct oracle to generate verified test cases improves correctness and performance over self-debugging and direct test generation.
The paper is well organized, with detailed experimental setup, prompt templates, case studies, and released code/data, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core idea of constructing optimization pairs by aggregating multiple users' submissions and sorting by runtime is relatively straightforward; novelty may be incremental, and the paper does not sufficiently compare against other multi-solution or retrieval-based fine-tuning strategies.

PCO is constructed by retaining the same number of pairs as PIE per problem but selecting those with top speedup ranking, which may bias the dataset toward easier or higher-difference pairs. Comparisons against PIE may therefore partly reflect this selection rather than the problem-oriented perspective alone.

Anchor verification still relies on LLM-generated test inputs and a single refinement iteration; correctness remains far from perfect, and the robustness/coverage of generated tests is not deeply evaluated. It is unclear how well it generalizes to other problem types or real-world code.

The evaluation is limited to C++ competitive programming problems from CodeNet/PIE and focuses only on runtime optimization; generalization to other languages, memory optimization, real-world software, and larger projects is not shown.

Baselines are somewhat narrow: self-debugging and direct test generation are compared, but other test-generation, execution-feedback, or data-selection methods are not. Statistical significance of gains is also not reported.

The paper's broader impact may be moderate for a top-tier AI venue: the method is practical and empirically effective, but it is not a fundamental algorithmic advance, and the limitations reduce confidence in wide applicability.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated core idea: the problem-oriented perspective (pooling submissions for the same problem across users, sorted by runtime) is simple but yields large, consistent empirical gains, and the motivation (single-programmer cognitive inertia) is convincingly argued and supported by GED, semantic embedding, and human/LLM analyses.

The Anchor Verification Framework is an elegant, task-specific insight: exploiting the 'slow but correct' pre-optimization code as a trusted test oracle is a genuinely novel application of execution feedback in code optimization (as opposed to error-prone synthetic test generation), and the two-step input-then-output construction is well justified by the 'Comparison Group' ablation (Table 3).

Evaluation is broad and multi-faceted: 5+ base models and scales (CodeLlama 13B, DeepSeekCoder 7B/33B, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B/32B, GPT-4/4o, DeepSeek-V3), Best@1 and Best@8, plus Python cross-language replication, quantum of iterations, Best@k cost/benefit, and a physical-hardware validation (Pearson 0.89 with gem5).

Good ablations distinguishing perspective from selection: PCO-Random vs. PCO-Top-Speedup vs. PIE (Table 6) isolates the effect of the data-construction perspective from the sampling heuristic, and the GED-stratified subsets (Table 12) test the mechanism behind the gains (high-GED pairs help, not hurt).

Honest and thorough treatment of the 'optimization tax' issue: the paper documents the correctness-efficiency trade-off, quantifies it, provides a failure-mode analysis (Table 7: 53% semantic errors), and demonstrates the anchor framework consistently improves %OPT, SPEEDUP, and CORRECT simultaneously across language (C++ and Python).

Reproducibility is reasonable: dataset statistics (Table 5), LoRA fine-tuning configuration, GPU hours, optimizer/learning rate, full prompt templates for all methods (Figures 8-15), and implementation details for baselines.
weaknesses: The central 'problem-oriented perspective' contribution is fundamentally a re-organization of an existing dataset (PIE/CodeNet) by sorting submissions per problem and pairing across users; the algorithm is arguably incremental, and the paper itself calls it 'simple but not trivial'. Much of the reported gain may be attributable to (a) a larger/denser set of optimization pairs and (b) a selection bias toward larger speedups (PCO-Top-Speedup), rather than a fundamentally new method.

The evaluation domain is limited to competitive-programming problems from CodeNet, whose solutions are short, self-contained, and heavily represented in public training corpora; the generalization to real-world codebases discussed in Section 4 is entirely speculative and unsupported by experiments. Potential benchmark contamination from CodeNet is not analyzed.

The Anchor Verification Framework assumes the 'slow code' is functionally correct, which is generally true for accepted CodeNet submissions but is not a safe assumption in real-world settings (the paper acknowledges only partial accuracy, but does not test the case of a faulty anchor). Test coverage is also thin: only 3 LLM-generated test inputs per problem (Appendix Q), which may limit the validity of the 'verified' test cases.

Comparisons for the anchor framework are limited to Self-Debugging and Direct Test Generation, and to at most 5 refinement iterations. More sophisticated code-generation refinement/test-automation baselines (e.g., self-consistency over candidates, existing test-synthesis+repair pipelines, CodeT-style filtering, or AlphaCode-style post-selection) are not compared, and the reported CORRECT values (~60-75%) leave substantial room for error, suggesting the framework is not yet a robust solution to the correctness problem.

The human/LLM optimization-type analyses are performed on small samples (100 pairs for human analysis; Figure 7 for LLM analysis), which weakens the strength of the claims about global vs. local optimization distributions, and the observed discrepancy between GPT-4 and human labeling is only briefly discussed.

Some claims are stronger than the supporting evidence, e.g., 'leading to significant improvements... to new levels', and the framing of 'Finding 2' (that %OPT and CORRECT converge on PCO) is interesting but only briefly explored. The broader significance of the approach with respect to existing optimization literature (compilers, automated algorithm selection) is treated lightly.

strengths: The empirical finding that a problem-oriented construction of optimization pairs—ordering all users' submissions for the same problem by runtime rather than following a single user's iterations—substantially outperforms the user-oriented PIE construction is interesting and non-obvious, and it is supported by a clean ablation (PCO-Random vs. PIE vs. PCO-Top-Speedup) that isolates the 'perspective' effect from the 'pair-selection' effect.

The evaluation is broad and thorough: multiple LLM families (CodeLLaMA, DeepSeekCoder, Qwen2.5-Coder), two programming languages (C++ and Python, Appendix J), a physical-hardware validation of the gem5-based speedups (Appendix P), GED-stratified and PCO-percentage ablations, and cost/scaling studies for BEST@k.

The anchor verification framework is a principled and clean use of the observation that the pre-optimization 'slow' code is functionally correct, allowing it to serve as a reliable test-case oracle; it is benchmarked against sensible baselines (self-debugging and direct test generation) and shown to improve %OPT, SPEEDUP, and CORRECT simultaneously.

Reproducibility is well supported by detailed prompts (Appendices M, Q), hyperparameters, failure-mode analysis, and qualitative case studies, making the experimental claims easy to scrutinize and replicate.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The 'problem-oriented perspective' is essentially a re-sorting/re-partitioning of the existing PIE dataset, and the 'anchor verification framework' is a form of test-case-based iterative refinement using the correct code as an oracle. Neither constitutes a substantive conceptual advance over prior work (e.g., Shypula et al., 2024), so the contribution is largely empirical and dataset-engineering rather than a new modeling or algorithmic idea.

The claims are substantially stronger than the evidence. Phrases such as 'completely different perspective,' 'significantly enhances ... to new levels,' and 'novel ... framework' oversell a modest conceptual delta and risk misleading readers about the depth of the contribution.

No comparison against more capable code-optimization/refinement baselines (e.g., RL-based, search/agent-based, or iterative-repair methods). The only refinement baselines are self-debugging and direct test generation, so the framework's advantage relative to the broader space of optimization approaches is unclear.

Several analyses are largely descriptive and confirm near-tautological expectations. The GED histogram and t-SNE clustering (Figures 2–3) mainly show that different programmers write different code, which adds little mechanistic insight into why the problem-oriented perspective helps beyond the qualitative 'diversity of thought' narrative.

The anchor verification stage relies on only three LLM-generated test inputs (Stage 1) that are then executed against the slow code. Three cases is a very weak verification signal for correctness, and the paper does not analyze how sensitive the results are to the number/quality of generated tests, nor whether the evaluation test suite overlaps with the verification cases.

No statistical significance or variance reporting. Results are reported as single BEST@k numbers, and the BEST@k pipeline uses test cases as an oracle to select candidates, which may overstate the practical applicability of the reported gains.

The reported gains arise primarily from how the training data is constructed/selected rather than from improved modeling; the mechanism (global algorithmic vs. local edits) is only analyzed at a high level, and combining Pairwise Ordinal Comparisons with the anchor framework does not clearly demonstrate that the LLM has learned transferable optimization skill rather than fitting the distribution of top-speedup pairs.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated, and useful conceptual contribution: the shift from a user-oriented to a problem-oriented perspective for constructing code optimization pairs. The construction is simple but well-justified, and the data-scarcity scaling argument (C(Σn,2) vs ΣC(n,2)) is mathematically clean and compelling.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing: five code LLMs (CodeLLAMA 13B, DeepSeekCoder 7B/33B, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B/32B), prompting baselines (Instruct/CoT), Best@1/Best@8, coupled with large and consistent improvements (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder 32B %OPT 31.24%→58.90%, Speedup 2.95×→5.22×).

The analysis is unusually thorough and multi-faceted: structural (Graph Edit Distance of CFGs), semantic (t-SNE of CodeT5+ embeddings), human and LLM categorization of optimization types, data-efficiency analysis, and failure-mode analysis. These support the central claims rather than only reporting headline metrics.

Well-designed ablations that isolate the true source of gains: the PIE / PCO-Random / PCO-Top-Speedup comparison convincingly shows that the problem-oriented perspective itself (not selection bias toward high-speedup pairs) drives the improvement, and the GED-stratified analysis shows high-disparity (algorithmic) pairs help rather than hurt learning.

The Anchor Verification Framework is a sensible and practical use of the task structure ('slow but correct' code as a trustworthy test oracle). It improves %OPT, Speedup, and Correct simultaneously (e.g., DeepSeek-V3 Correct 61.55%→74.54%) and is properly compared against Self-Debugging and Direct Test Generation, with a root-cause analysis of the effect of using executed vs. LLM-synthesized outputs.

Strong reproducibility and transparency: prompts, hyperparameters (LoRA config, epochs, optimizer, learning rate), training cost (GPU hours), token-cost trade-off analysis for Best@k, and failure analyses are all provided, and generalization to Python plus validation on physical hardware strengthen external validity.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, and it includes an honest limitations section acknowledging that time-only optimization and residual correctness errors remain open problems.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate. The problem-oriented perspective is essentially a re-grouping/re-ordering of an existing dataset (PIE) rather than a fundamentally new method or model, and the Anchor Verification Framework substantially overlaps with existing execution-feedback / test-case-generation refinement pipelines (Chen et al. 2023, 2024a; Wei et al. 2024). The distinguishing element—using the original slow code as the oracle—is a neat trick but arguably incremental.

The 'optimization tax' is only partially mitigated: even with anchoring, ~25% of optimized programs remain incorrect on the PCO baseline, so the framing of 'unlocking' performance could be tempered and the practical usefulness for correctness-critical settings is still limited.

The dataset base is CodeNet, which is a single competitive-programming corpus. Despite the Python extension and hardware check (only 20 pairs), the evidence for generalizability to realistic, large-scale software engineering codebases relies on a discussion rather than empirical demonstration, weakening the real-world significance claim.

The evaluation is predominantly on the gem5 simulator, and the physical-hardware validation is small (20 pairs, single microarchitecture). The systematic -11.6% gap suggests simulator numbers may overstate absolute speedups, though relative trends are preserved.

The anchor-framework comparison is restricted to two refinement baselines at a fixed iteration budget and a single dataset; a comparison to broader/stronger refinement or compiler-based (e.g., -O3-aware) baselines would better situate the gains.

Some results are reported only at Best@1, and the Correct drops observed for several models under Best@8 on PCO (though explained by the authors) suggest the optimization/correctness trade-off is not fully characterized, and the selection of 'best' by fastest-passing-test could be an optimistic upper bound relative to what is achievable without a ground-truth oracle.
